newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Novartis growth flags in Q2.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Novartis growth flags in Q2.

text.p: Novartis AG reported on Thursday a 19 percent rise in first half group sales, but the share price dipped as the market digested flagging second quarter sales growth.

First half sales for the life sciences group, formed last year through the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz, totalled 16.56 billion Swiss francs ($11.2 billion) against 13.89 billion for the corresponding 1996 period.
The figures reflect a six percent local currency increase in the second quarter, down from 14 percent rise in the first three months of the year.
Although the overall sales performance was in line with expectations, lower-than-expected sales from the key drugs segment met with disappointment on the market.

"The overall figure of seven percent shows a slowdown which was slightly disappointing for me," Union Bancaire Privee analyst Romain Pasche said, adding, "The source of the slowdown was mainly healthcare."
At midsession, Novartis' share price was down 32 francs at 2,414 on the Swiss Exchange.
For the first half, pharmaceutical sales totalled 6.93 billion francs, an increase of 23 percent in Swiss francs but just 10 percent in local currencies.
The comparison was not flattered by the particularly strong performance the first half of 1996, analysts said.

Bank Vontobel analyst Susanne Borer noted that local currency sales growth for Sandimmun and Neoral, the group's transplantation and auto-immune drugs, was only five percent in the first half compared to 14 percent for the same 1996 period.

The company said in its first half statement that sales growth in pharma was driven by dynamic performance in the U.S., Europe and Spain. But sales in Japan and Germany were hurt by government measures to cut healthcare costs.
Sales of Over-The-Counter (OTC) products, which were four percent lower, were damaged by poor European demand, especially in Germany due to new reimbursement regulations.

However, slower second quarter growth in pharmaceuticals was partly offset by strong expansion of the group's nutrition business, which posted sales of 2.08 billion, representing a 19 percent Swiss franc rise and a six percent increase in local currencies.
"We had expected growth of 15 percent and three percent (respectively)," Borer said.
Novartis said its infant and baby nutrition business was driven by an "outstanding" performance in Eastern Europe, Central and Latin America.
Analysts were divided on their near-term outlook for the company.

Romain Pasche of Union Bancaire Privee found the growth slowdown slightly disappointing, and said he may downgrade his profit forecasts. Pasche has forecast first half net profit of 2.87 billion francs and a full-year figure of 5.47 billion.
But UBS analyst Birgit Kulhoff said she was maintaining a "buy" recommendation for Novartis and a 1997 net profit forecast of 5.28 billion.
"We still think a 10 percent underlying growth rate is feasible for Novartis," she said.
Moving to the group's other business segments, seed sales were 23 percent higher in Swiss francs at 1.03 billion francs, a local currency rise of nine percent.
Group agribusiness sales were 16 percent higher in Swiss francs, and up four percent in local currencies, at 5.29 billion.
Nutrition sales were up 19 percent and six percent respectively, at 2.08 billion francs. ($ = 1.484 Swiss Francs)
